authors: Banks MS, Sprague WW, Schmoll J, Parnell JAQ, Love GD
title: Why do animal eyes have pupils of different shapes? (supplementary materials: table S1, list of species with pupil shapes; tables S2 to S4)
why: Table S1 gives the pupil shape of each of 214 species, which would set the pupil for pumas, cheetahs, leopards, jaguars, bobcats, coyotes and gray foxes; the page and its supplement could not be reached from this machine.

title: Über die Sehschärfe des Haushundes bei verschiedenen Helligkeiten
journal: cited by Beltran et al. 2014 (PLoS ONE 9: e90390, ref. 57) as Zentralbl Vergleich Physiol 57: 137-146
why: Dog acuity measured at several light levels would set how the dog view sharpens and blurs as the light changes in the proposed night shift.

title: Retinal photoreceptor and ganglion cell types and topographies in the red fox (Vulpes vulpes) and Arctic fox (Vulpes lagopus)
why: The full text estimates acuity for both foxes from ganglion cell density and eye size, which would replace the fox view's guessed sharpness and set its streak weights.

title: Visual acuity in mammals: effects of eye size and ecology (online supplementary table 1)
why: The supplementary table lists acuity by species and method, which would give measured values for big cats, wolves and foxes in place of the eye-size inference.

title: The luminance dependence of spatial vision in the cat
why: Cat acuity and contrast sensitivity across light levels would set how the cat view sharpens and blurs with the light in the proposed night shift, as Lind et al. 2017 do for dogs.

authors: Coile DC, Pollitz CH, Smith JC
title: Behavioral determination of critical flicker fusion in dogs
why: Gives the dog's flicker limit (75 Hz in a review) with its light level and method, which sets the dog view's pace.

title: Temporal modulation sensitivity of the cat: I. Behavioral methods
journal: Vision Research 15: 555-561 (as cited by Inger et al. 2014, ref. 62, which prints the second author as Berkeley MS)
why: Would settle whether the cat's 47.5 Hz flicker limit is behavioural or ERG and at what light level, which decides whether the cat view needs any time effect.

title: Movement detection by cats: invariance with direction and target configuration
journal: Journal of Comparative and Physiological Psychology 94: 943-952
why: The cat's own velocity threshold would replace the 1 to 10 degrees a second range that covers cats, rats and pigeons together.

title: The effects of time, luminance, and high contrast targets: revisiting grating acuity in the domestic cat
why: Cat grating acuity against luminance and time would set the cat view's sharpness by light level.

title: Neutral point testing of color vision in the domestic cat
why: A behavioural neutral point for cats would test the deutan colour matrix the cat view uses.

title: Topography of ganglion cells in the dog and wolf retina
why: Density maps for seven breeds and the wolf would set the weights of the streak and the central spot in the dog view's nose setting.

authors: McGreevy P, Grassi TD, Harman AM
title: A strong correlation exists between the distribution of retinal ganglion cells and nose length in the dog
why: The breed-by-breed table of streak and area centralis would let the nose setting follow skull length.

title: (title not shown in the part of the citing review that opened)
journal: Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association 207: 1623-1634, as cited by Byosiere et al. 2018
why: The primary review behind the dog's 20/75 acuity, 240 degree field and 30 to 60 degree overlap, which the dog rows now take from secondary sources.

authors: Odom JV, Bromberg NM, Dawson WW
title: Canine visual acuity: retinal and cortical field potentials evoked by pattern stimulation
journal: American Journal of Physiology 245: R637-R641 (as cited by Beltran et al. 2014, ref. 59)
why: Source of the 12.6 cycles per degree upper estimate of dog acuity.

authors: Murphy CJ, Mutti DO, Zadnik K, Ver Hoeve J
title: Effect of optical defocus on visual acuity in dogs
journal: American Journal of Veterinary Research 58: 414-418 (as cited by Beltran et al. 2014, ref. 60)
why: Behavioural dog acuity (20/45 to 20/85) and the cost of defocus, which bears on the dog view's sharpness and depth blur.

authors: Ahnelt PK, Schubert C, Kübber-Heiss A, Schiviz AN, Anger E
title: Independent variation of retinal S and M cone photoreceptor topographies: a survey of four families of mammals
why: Cone maps of the lion, tiger, cheetah and lynx would set where the big-cat and lynx views are sharpest.

title: Animal Eyes, 2nd edition: chapter 5, Lens eyes on land
why: The owner's copy came through only to p. 65; this chapter treats pupils and lenses of land vertebrates, for the slit-pupil and multifocal-lens rows.

title: Animal Eyes, 2nd edition: chapter 6, Mirrors in animals (the tapetum)
why: Would say whether a tapetum costs sharpness, which decides the eyeshine effect proposed for the night shift; the DOI is the book's, as the chapter's own was not seen.

title: Animal Eyes, 2nd edition: chapter 9, Movements of the eyes
why: Background on how mammals move their eyes, for a future gaze effect in the cat and dog views.

authors: Gunter R, Harding HGW, Stiles WS
title: Spectral reflexion factor of the cat's tapetum
why: The tapetum's reflectance spectrum would set the tint of the proposed eyeshine glow.

title: The relative importance of the distance senses in coyote predatory behaviour
why: Would say how much coyotes, the most recorded canid after the red fox, rely on sight against hearing and smell when hunting, for a coyote row in the dog view.
